bar.name: Bar
bar.useWhen: You are comparing values across separate categories.
bar.description: Every bar starts from the same baseline, so the eye compares lengths accurately.
bar.example: Average quiz score for each of five class sections.
bar.tip: Start the value axis at zero, and sort the bars when the order of the categories does not matter.

groupedBar.name: Grouped Bar
groupedBar.useWhen: You are showing how each category changed between two or three periods or groups.
groupedBar.description: Side-by-side bars put the before and after values for each category next to each other.
groupedBar.example: Enrollment in four courses, last year compared with this year.
groupedBar.tip: Keep to two or three bars per group. More than that turns into a picket fence.
groupedBar.sampleTitle: Enrollment by course: last year vs. this year

stackedBar.name: Stacked Bar
stackedBar.useWhen: You are showing what the total for each category is made of.
stackedBar.description: Each bar is a total, and its colored segments show the parts that add up to it.
stackedBar.example: Survey answers (agree, neutral, disagree) for each grade level.
stackedBar.tip: Only the bottom segment sits on a flat baseline, so put the most important part there.

line.name: Line
line.useWhen: You are comparing values at different points in time, or comparing several series over time.
line.description: Connecting the points lets the slope of the line show how fast the value is rising or falling.
line.example: Monthly test averages for two schools.
line.tip: Time always runs left to right on the horizontal axis.
line.sampleTitle: Monthly test average for two schools

area.name: Area
area.useWhen: You want to stress how much a single quantity rose or fell over time.
area.description: An area chart is a line chart with the space under the line filled in, which draws attention to volume.
area.example: Daily website visits over a year.
area.tip: Use it for one series. Several overlapping areas hide each other.

stackedArea.name: Stacked Area
stackedArea.useWhen: You are showing how the parts of a total change over time.
stackedArea.description: The top edge shows the total, and each colored band shows one part's contribution.
stackedArea.example: Monthly sales for three product lines.
stackedArea.tip: Only the bottom band and the total are easy to read precisely.
stackedArea.sampleTitle: Monthly sales for three product lines

dualAxis.name: Dual Axis
dualAxis.useWhen: You are showing two measures with different units over the same time span.
dualAxis.description: Bars use the left axis and the line uses the right axis, so two different units share one chart.
dualAxis.example: Daily temperature and ice cream sales over one summer.
dualAxis.tip: Use with care: the two scales are arbitrary, so the places where the bars and the line cross mean nothing. A scatter plot is often clearer.

histogram.name: Histogram
histogram.useWhen: You are showing how the values of one variable are spread out.
histogram.description: Values are sorted into bins, and the height of each bar shows how many values fell into that bin.
histogram.example: Quiz scores for 200 students grouped into ten-point bins.
histogram.tip: Try a few bin widths. Too few bins hide the shape, and too many add noise.

scatter.name: Scatter
scatter.useWhen: You are checking whether two numeric variables are related.
scatter.description: Each dot is one observation, placed by its value on each of the two variables.
scatter.example: Hours studied compared with exam score for each student.
scatter.tip: Add a trend line to show the pattern, and remember that correlation is not causation.

pie.name: Pie / Donut
pie.useWhen: You are showing a few parts of one whole.
pie.description: The full circle is 100 percent, and each slice shows one part's share.
pie.example: A school budget split among four departments.
pie.tip: Often misused: keep to five slices or fewer, and never use a pie to compare values that are close together.

boxPlot.name: Box Plot
boxPlot.useWhen: You are comparing the spread of several groups.
boxPlot.description: Each box shows the middle half of the values, the line inside it is the median, and the whiskers show the range.
boxPlot.example: Reaction times for three age groups.
boxPlot.tip: A box plot packs a whole distribution into five numbers, which makes groups easy to compare.
boxPlot.sampleTitle: Reaction time for three age groups

violin.name: Violin
violin.useWhen: You want to show the full shape of the distribution for each group.
violin.description: The width of each violin shows how common the values are at that height.
violin.example: Score distributions for three teaching methods.
violin.tip: A violin plot reveals two-peaked data that a box plot hides.

treemap.name: Treemap
treemap.useWhen: You are showing many parts of one whole, or parts inside parts.
treemap.description: The whole rectangle is 100 percent, and the area of each tile shows one part's share.
treemap.example: Storage space used by each folder on a drive.
treemap.tip: A treemap stays readable when a pie chart would have too many slices.

bubble.name: Bubble
bubble.useWhen: You are relating two variables while a third variable sets the size of each point.
bubble.description: A bubble chart is a scatter plot where the size of each dot carries an extra measure.
bubble.example: Study hours compared with score, with each bubble sized by class size.
bubble.tip: Size the bubbles by area, not by radius, or large values will look far too big.
bubble.sampleTitle: Hours vs. score, sized by class size

heatmap.name: Heatmap
heatmap.useWhen: You are showing how often pairs of values occur across two dimensions.
heatmap.description: Each cell is colored by its value, so clusters and gaps show up as dark and light patches.
heatmap.example: Learner activity by day of the week and hour of the day.
heatmap.tip: Use one color that runs from light to dark so that darker always means more.
heatmap.sampleTitle: Activity by weekday and time of day

pieBad.name: Pie for comparing
pieBad.useWhen: A pie chart is a poor tool for comparing values that are close together.
pieBad.description: People judge angles and areas far less accurately than lengths, so similar slices look the same.
pieBad.example: Which of these five slices is the largest? It is hard to tell.
pieBad.tip: Treat the parts as categories and use a Bar chart instead (Categorical row, Compare values column).

scenarios.text: Five class sections took the same quiz. You want to show which section had the highest average.
You recorded website visits every day for a year and want to show how the number of visits rose and fell.
You have quiz scores for 200 students and want to see whether most scores cluster near the middle.
For each student you know the hours studied and the exam score. Do students who study more score higher?
A school budget is split among four departments. You want to show each department's share of the total.
Survey results are split by grade level, and each grade's answers are divided into agree, neutral and disagree. Show the makeup of each grade's answers.
You have monthly sales for three product lines and want to show how each line added to the total over two years.
You want to show enrollment in four courses last year next to enrollment this year, so readers can see how each course changed.
You have daily temperature and daily ice cream sales for one summer and want both measures on one chart over time.
